title: Power Banks for Power Outages: What They Can Charge, What They Can't, and Three to Consider
subtitle: A charged-up battery pack can keep your phone going when the lights go out, as long as you know its limits and fill it up ahead of time.
excerpt: When the power goes out, a charged phone helps you stay in touch. Here is how a simple battery pack works, what it cannot run, and three Anker models with posted prices.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: When a storm knocks out the power, the first thing many of us reach for is the phone. It is how we call family, check on neighbors and follow the weather. The trouble is that a phone battery does not last forever, and the wall outlet is no help when the house is dark.
A power bank is a simple fix. It is a battery in a small box that you charge ahead of time, then plug your phone into when you need it. Consumer Reports notes that a power pack needs no gas or fuel.
How a power bank works, and what it cannot do
Think of it like a water jug. You fill it from the wall while the power is on. Later, you pour that stored energy into your phone or tablet through a charging cable.

Two numbers matter most. The first is capacity, written in mAh (milliamp-hours, a measure of how much energy the battery holds). Bigger means more phone charges. Consumer Reports (https://www.consumerreports.org/electronics-computers/portable-chargers/best-portable-chargers-power-banks-of-the-year-a1159301636/) says capacity is one of the most important factors, and that a 10,000mAh charger is likely a good fit for everyday phone charging: compact, light and good for at least a couple of charges.
The second is watts (W), which tells you how fast power flows out. A low number is fine for a phone, but it is slow for a laptop.

Now the honest part. A power bank is not a generator. It will not run a refrigerator, a space heater, an oxygen machine, a CPAP machine or other medical equipment. It is meant to keep a phone, and maybe a tablet or small laptop, running for a while. The advertised capacity is also a best case. Real-world charges come out fewer, because phone batteries vary.

"...you can charge it before there's a power outage" — Paul Hope, Consumer Reports, quoted by WESH (https://www.wesh.com/article/best-portable-chargers-hurricane-season-consumer-reports/71510425), June 2026
That is the whole point, and also the catch. A power bank needs electricity to refill itself, so an empty one is no help once the lights are already out.

items: Capacity that fits your needs: Consumer Reports says 10,000mAh is likely a good fit for everyday phone charging. Larger packs, like the 20,000mAh and 24,000mAh models below, hold more but take longer to recharge themselves.
Weight: bigger batteries are heavier. The 10,000mAh Anker below weighs 7.5 ounces, while the 24,000mAh Anker 737 weighs 22.22 ounces.
Ports and cables: check that the pack has the type of plug your phone uses. A built-in cable means one less thing to lose in a dark drawer.
Wattage if you have a laptop: a pack with low output (around 15W) will charge a laptop slowly. Higher-wattage packs are faster, though speed also depends on your device and cable.
Recharge time: larger packs take longer to fill back up, so plan ahead.
Extra fees: you do not need a membership to buy a power bank. Anker's pages also promote optional Anker Plus memberships, so skip any add-on offers unless you have read the terms.
Returns and warranty: look for a money-back window so you can send it back if it does not suit you. The Anker pages below list a 30-day money-back guarantee.

sections.content: Getting it ready before the next storm
Charge your power bank fully before a storm is expected, not after the power is already out. Keep it with the right charging cable for your phone, so you are not hunting for parts in the dark.
Batteries get warm. Follow the instructions in the manual for storing and recharging, and replace any pack that is old or looks swollen.

If you travel, a general rule is that airlines and shippers limit lithium batteries, and they should go in your carry-on bag rather than checked luggage. This rule is not from the sources above, so check with your airline before you fly.

If you or someone you care for relies on a CPAP, oxygen or any other powered medical device, a phone power bank is not the answer. Ask your doctor or the equipment supplier about a proper backup plan, and check the device's power needs before counting on any battery.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A power bank will not keep the whole house running, but it can keep your phone going for a while. Pick one that fits your needs and put it somewhere easy to find, so it is ready when you need it.

products.name: Anker 313 Power Bank (PowerCore 10K)
products.price: $25.99 (price on Anker's product page; check current price)
products.blurb: A slim, 7.5-ounce, 10,000mAh pack for anyone who mainly needs to keep a phone going. Anker's page says, "It can charge a phone up to three times and most tablets once." That is marketing copy, and real results vary. Its 15W USB-C output is slow for laptops.

products.name: Anker Power Bank (20K, 87W, Built-In USB-C Cable)
products.price: $69.99 (price on Anker's product page; check current price)
products.blurb: A 20,000mAh middle choice for households with a phone and a tablet, with a built-in USB-C cable so there is nothing to misplace. It shares 87W of total output across up to three devices, and a single device can receive up to 65W.

products.name: Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K)
products.price: $109.99 (price on Anker's product page; Anker's emergency-power page lists $98.99 on sale, so check current price in your cart)
products.blurb: A 24,000mAh pack with 140W maximum total output, for people who want higher output, which can suit laptops depending on the laptop's needs. It weighs 22.22 ounces and has two USB-C outputs and one USB-A.
